opus-5.5.text:
I think for developers, the biggest value is predictability. When you're building a product on top of a model, you want to know how it's going to behave, not just in the common cases but in the edge cases too. The Model Spec tries to lay that out explicitly: here's how the model is supposed to weigh instructions from the developer versus the user, here's what it will and won't do by default, and here's what you can customize.

One of the core ideas is the chain of command. Developers can set instructions in the system or developer message, and the model is meant to follow those within the bounds we set, while users can adjust things within the space the developer allows. So if you're building, say, a customer support bot or a tutoring app, the spec helps you understand how much latitude you have to shape the model's persona, tone, scope, and so on, and where the hard limits are that no instruction will override.

It's also useful when something goes wrong. If the model does something unexpected, you can go back to the spec and ask: is this a bug, meaning the model isn't following the spec, or is this intended behavior that I need to work around or configure differently? That gives developers a shared vocabulary with us, and it makes feedback much more actionable. If you can point to a specific principle and say, "the model isn't doing this," that's really helpful for us to improve training.

And more broadly, we publish it because we think transparency matters. Developers are making real decisions about whether and how to deploy these models, and they deserve to know what we're aiming for, not just discover it through trial and error.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I think about the Model Spec for developers is that it's really a contract. When you're building on top of a model, the thing you need most is predictability. You need to know how the model is going to behave by default, where the boundaries are, and which of those boundaries you're allowed to move.

The Spec lays that out explicitly. It describes a chain of command: there are things the platform sets that can't be overridden, there are defaults that developers can adjust, and there are defaults that end users can adjust. So if you're a developer and you're wondering, "Can I tell the model to only answer questions about my product? Can I turn off the hedging? Can I have it adopt a persona?" the answer isn't a guess anymore. You can go read it.

The second thing it does is make our reasoning legible. Before the Spec, if the model refused something or responded in a way you didn't expect, it felt like a black box. Now you can look at the document and say, okay, that behavior traces back to this principle, and here's the example that illustrates it. That makes it much easier to design your system prompt around how the model actually works rather than fighting it.

And the third piece is that it gives developers a way to push back. The Spec is public, and we update it. When developers say, "This default doesn't make sense for my use case, here's why," that feedback feeds into the next version. So it's not just documentation, it's the surface where we negotiate what the model should do. For people building real products, that's a lot more useful than having to reverse-engineer the behavior from trial and error.

astra-6.text:
I think the Model Spec is useful to developers in a couple of ways. First, it gives them a clearer picture of the behavior we’re trying to train into the models. When you build a product around a model, you need to understand how it will interpret your instructions, how it will handle conflicting instructions, and when it might ask a clarifying question or decline a request. The spec gives you a framework for reasoning about those things.

Second, it helps clarify where developers can customize behavior for their application and where there are shared boundaries. You can use that to design your instructions and your evaluations, and to make sense of unexpected responses.

That doesn’t mean every model response perfectly follows the spec. It’s a statement of intended behavior. But having that written down makes it easier to identify gaps and have a concrete conversation about what should improve.

I think the Model Spec gives developers a clearer picture of how we intend our models to behave. When you’re building a product around a model, you need to understand how it will follow instructions, handle conflicting requests, and respond when it can’t help with something.

Having that written down gives developers a shared reference for designing their applications and evaluating the responses they get. It’s a statement of intended behavior, rather than a guarantee that every response will be perfect, but it makes those expectations more explicit and gives us something concrete to improve against.
